name: The AI Enablement Audit in Healthcare
title: The AI Enablement Audit in Healthcare
answer: An AI enablement audit in healthcare is a structured review of how artificial intelligence systems are selected, deployed, and maintained within a clinical or operational setting. It covers model inventory, intended use, data flows, integration points, and the human oversight attached to each system. The audit distinguishes between general-purpose tools, regulated medical devices, and research or administrative models, and it maps each to the clinical workflow it touches. Its purpose is to give an organization a current, defensible picture of where AI is active and where it is not.

sections.body: An AI enablement audit in healthcare is a structured review of how artificial intelligence systems are selected, deployed, and maintained within a clinical or operational setting. It covers model inventory, intended use, data flows, integration points, and the human oversight attached to each system. The audit distinguishes between general-purpose tools, regulated medical devices, and research or administrative models, and it maps each to the clinical workflow it touches. Its purpose is to give an organization a current, defensible picture of where AI is active and where it is not.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The audit runs on the same infrastructure that hosts the AI systems: electronic health record integrations, cloud or on-premises model endpoints, data pipelines, and access control logs. It also draws on procurement records, vendor documentation, and configuration management databases to establish what is actually running. For regulated devices, the audit checks the installed software version, the intended use statement, and the change control history. No special hardware is required, but reliable logging and a complete asset inventory are prerequisites.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done through document review, structured interviews with clinical and technical owners, and direct inspection of model registries and system settings. Auditors compare each AI system against its cleared or claimed purpose, its training data provenance, and its performance monitoring plan. They look for gaps between what a vendor says a model does and how it is configured in practice, including silent updates, disabled alerts, or off-label use. Findings are usually recorded in a risk register with a severity rating and an owner.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk in this audit center on patient safety, data protection, and liability. The audit checks whether each AI system has a lawful basis for processing patient data, whether consent or opt-out mechanisms are respected, and whether adverse events or near misses are reported through the correct channels. It also reviews contracts for indemnification, audit rights, and data retention, because responsibility for a model's output often sits between the vendor and the care provider. The site's tracking of active product liability and wrongful death lawsuits against AI companies is a reminder that these are not abstract risks.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The audit is moving from a one-time project to a continuous process, with automated model inventories and real-time drift monitoring becoming standard. Regulators are paying closer attention to post-market performance, so future audits will likely require evidence of ongoing validation rather than a snapshot at deployment. Healthcare organizations are also starting to audit generative AI tools used for documentation and patient communication, which brings new questions about accuracy, bias, and clinician review. The direction is toward an audit trail that can be shown to a regulator or a court without additional reconstruction.
